title: India Directs ONGC to Build $1.6 Billion Strategic Oil Reserve as Iran War Exposes Eight-Day Vulnerability
excerpt: The new underground cavern at Mangaluru would raise India's emergency crude storage by a third, but still leaves the country far short of the IEA's 90-day standard
body:
India's government has directed state-owned Oil and Natural Gas Corporation to build a new strategic petroleum reserve facility in Mangaluru, Karnataka, in what amounts to the country's most significant push to shore up emergency crude oil stockpiles in over a decade. The project, estimated to cost approximately $1.6 billion (₹13,000–14,000 crore), comes as the Iran war and its fallout across the Strait of Hormuz have laid bare just how thin India's energy cushion really is.

The directive, first reported by the Economic Times citing sources with knowledge of the plans, tasks ONGC with both constructing and filling a new underground cavern with a proposed capacity of 1.75 million metric tons of crude oil. Roughly ₹5,000 crore of the total cost would go toward building the cavern itself, with another ₹10,000 crore required to fill it at current oil prices.

Eight Days of Cover — and a Global Standard of Ninety

India's existing strategic petroleum reserves, managed by Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited (ISPRL), are spread across three underground facilities at Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh and at Mangaluru and Padur in Karnataka. Together, they hold 5.33 million metric tons of crude oil — equivalent to approximately 39 million barrels, or just eight days of the country's oil consumption at its current rate of roughly 5 million barrels per day.

That level of cover is strikingly low by international standards. The International Energy Agency recommends that member nations maintain reserves equivalent to at least 90 days of net imports. Even adjusting for India's non-IEA membership, the eight-day buffer leaves New Delhi dangerously exposed to supply disruptions — a vulnerability the Iran war brought into sharp relief as energy import bills soared and domestic fuel prices spiked.

The new Mangaluru cavern would raise total strategic capacity by approximately one-third to around 7 million metric tons. While meaningful, it would still cover only about 11 days of consumption — a fraction of what major economies like the United States, Japan, and South Korea hold in reserve.

> "The new Mangaluru cavern would raise total strategic capacity by approximately one-third to around 7 million metric tons."

Why ONGC, and Why Now

The decision to assign the project to ONGC marks a structural departure from previous SPR development. Earlier facilities were funded directly by the government through ISPRL. This time, ONGC has been asked to finance and build the cavern on its own balance sheet — a model that spreads the fiscal burden away from the exchequer while leveraging ONGC's existing land holdings at the Mangaluru site.

![Andhra Pradesh — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Tirumala_090615.jpg/3840px-Tirumala_090615.jpg)

The timing is driven by geopolitics. India imports roughly 88 percent of its crude oil requirements, and the Iran war disrupted flows through the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint through which a significant share of the world's seaborne crude passes. India's energy import bill climbed sharply in recent months, and the government faced pressure to insulate the economy from future shocks.

Globally, the conflict has triggered what Reuters describes as a race among oil-importing nations to bolster their reserves. India's move places it alongside other major consumers seeking to build deeper strategic buffers, though the gap between its current reserves and international norms remains wide.

Strategic Ambiguity on Commercial Use

One unresolved question is whether the new facility will be restricted to government-held strategic reserves or could also function as a commercial storage site. India's existing Mangaluru facility offers a precedent: Abu Dhabi's ADNOC stores crude in one of its caverns under a commercial agreement, retaining the right to sell oil to Indian refineries during normal times while giving the Indian government access to the entire stockpile during emergencies.

A hybrid model could attract investment from international oil companies or sovereign wealth funds, offsetting some of ONGC's construction costs while keeping India's strategic interests protected.

The Diaspora Dimension

For the estimated 32 million-strong Indian diaspora, India's energy security is not an abstract policy concern. Supply shocks ripple through the economy in ways that touch NRI families directly — from rising prices of cooking gas and petrol that affect relatives in India, to inflationary pressure on food and transport that erodes the purchasing power of remittances.

Diaspora investors with exposure to Indian equities and real estate also feel the impact. Energy price spikes dampen GDP growth, weaken the rupee, and increase the current account deficit — all of which affect portfolio returns. The SPR expansion, while still modest by global standards, signals that New Delhi is treating energy resilience as a national security priority, a shift that could gradually reduce the volatility that has historically made India's economy sensitive to every tremor in the Persian Gulf.

The path from eight days of cover to anything resembling energy security is long and expensive — by one estimate, reaching the IEA's 90-day standard would require over 400 million additional barrels of storage at a cost north of $28 billion. But the Mangaluru project, for all its limitations, represents a concrete first step in a journey that the Iran war has made impossible to defer any longer.
